questions.q: What is the default governance state of a brand-new Azure subscription or AWS account, before any landing zone process touches it?
options: No logging, no shared network connectivity, no active policy guardrails, and no cost tagging by default
Fully logged, policy-enforced, and network-connected to shared services automatically
Locked down entirely until a support ticket is manually approved by the cloud provider
Automatically placed into the same compliance scope as every other account in the organization
questions.explain: A new subscription or account ships with cloud compute and storage primitives only — governance, logging, networking, and policy are not bundled in by the provider; they have to be added deliberately.

questions.q: Why does retrofitting governance (tagging, network segmentation, logging) onto an environment that already has resources running tend to cost more than building it in up front?
options: Retrofitting is actually cheaper, because existing resources can be reconfigured in bulk with no risk
Cloud providers charge an extra fee for applying policy to existing resources
The cost scales with how much has already been built without governance — more existing resources and teams means more to find, reconcile, and fix after the fact
It is impossible to add policy to a resource once it has been created
questions.explain: The guide's core point: the cost of adding governance is roughly proportional to how much already exists without it, so the cheapest point to add it is before anything is built.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a landing zone?
options: A single Azure or AWS product you install once and never touch again
A pre-provisioned, pre-governed environment that a new workload lands into, with identity, networking, policy, logging, and cost tracking already in place
A physical data center region where a cloud provider's servers are located
A firewall appliance placed at the edge of a virtual network
questions.explain: A landing zone is a pattern, not a product — the guide's building-lot analogy: roads, utilities, and a building code already in place before the first structure goes up.

questions.q: What are Azure Landing Zones and AWS Control Tower, relative to each other?
options: Competing standards that solve unrelated problems on each cloud
Azure Landing Zones is a subset of AWS Control Tower that only works for Azure-AWS hybrid deployments
Each vendor's own reference implementation of the same landing zone pattern, using different vocabulary for the same underlying governance problem
Legacy tools that have been fully replaced by Terraform modules
questions.explain: The guide is explicit: different vendor terms, same underlying answer to the same underlying problem — which is why Lessons 6 and 7 cover each one by name.

questions.q: Per the lesson, at what point does the landing zone pattern start paying for itself most clearly?
options: Only after a security incident has already occurred
Never — it is pure overhead with no measurable benefit
Only once an organization reaches enterprise scale with hundreds of accounts
The moment a second team needs cloud access, since each additional team can then inherit an already-built baseline instead of repeating manual setup
questions.explain: A single team on a single account can skip most of this with little risk, but the pattern compounds in value as soon as a second team is onboarded and inherits networking, logging, and policy automatically.
